title: Cour de Cassation curbs garde à vue extensions for minor offences
content: The Cour de Cassation ruled on Wednesday that extensions of *garde à vue* in minor-offence cases must rest on “concrete and individualised grounds” set out in writing by the procureur, closing a practice that had expanded since the 2019 amendment to the code of criminal procedure.

The *arrêt de principe*, adopted by the criminal chamber in a plenary formation, concerns a case in which a suspect was held for forty-two hours on a theft charge without a written justification beyond the standard reference to investigative needs. The court found the extension unlawful and annulled the subsequent statements.

The judgment does not change the statutory maximum, but it changes the practical test. Procureurs must now document why the ordinary duration is insufficient in each case, and the court indicates that generic references to “the complexity of the investigation” will not satisfy the requirement.

The barreau d’Aurelle, which supported the applicant, described the ruling as a correction long overdue. “The extension had become automatic; today it becomes exceptional again,” said Maître Odile Fargeon. The Conférence des procureurs said it would issue guidance before the end of the week, and the Parquet général is expected to circulate a *circulaire* to all jurisdictions.

The decision comes as the prison administration reports that *détention provisoire* accounts for 29 per cent of the incarcerated population, a figure that has risen steadily since 2020. Criminal lawyers argue that the two trends are linked: the longer a suspect is held in garde à vue, the more likely a juge d’instruction is to order pre-trial detention.

Victims’ associations warned that the ruling could slow investigations in organised theft networks, and asked the ministry to compensate with additional investigative resources rather than legislative reversal. The Ministry of Justice said it would study the arrêt before deciding whether to propose an amendment in the spring.
author: Étienne Bréart, chronique judiciaire — Agence des Républiques (ADR)
